title: Anchored batchlets fairness probe playbook
content:
Summary:

This doc records the design, runs, and early conclusions from the "anchored batchlets" probe — a set of continuous-batching scheduler experiments that try to reduce p99/p999 latency for latency-sensitive small requests while preserving overall token throughput. The idea: carve each scheduling slot into one or more anchored "batchlets" that guarantee a minimum flush cadence for older requests, combined with a probing mechanism that dynamically reweights fairness when backlog or latency signals spike.

Why we did this:
- Multiple customer reports + internal traces show long tail latency spikes during mixed workload bursts: lots of small, low-token requests interleaved with large-streaming generations.
- Existing timeouts and size thresholds either hurt throughput (flush too early) or hurt tail latency (wait too long for large batches).
- We want a deterministic, low-complexity primitive that programmers can reason about and operators can tune (anchors + probe weight).

Design overview (high level):
- Batchlet: a logical sub-batch formed inside a scheduling slot. A slot remains, but requests can be assigned to an "anchor" group. Each anchor has a target flush window (ms) and a minimum reservation of batch capacity (in tokens).
- Anchors prioritized by age and SLA class; older requests receive stronger anchoring.
- Probing mechanism: when internal latency metrics (p95/p99) exceed thresholds for two consecutive windows, scheduler increases fairness weight for anchors for N cycles (decay).
- Preemption: anchors may preempt non-anchored coalescence if soft-deadline approaches. Preemption is limited to X% of tokens per slot to bound throughput loss.

Hypotheses tested:
1) Anchors reduce p99 for small requests by ~30-50ms without hurting throughput more than 2-3%.
2) Probe-triggered fairness ramp recovers tail latency faster than static conservative settings (timeouts).
3) Heavy anchoring harms GPU utilization if reservation levels are too high; optimal anchor reservation is workload-dependent.

Testbed and workload mix:
- Hardware: 4x A100 80GB equivalent nodes, same runtime build as prod (2024-10-01).
- Load generator: synthetic traces + sampled production replay windows (3 hours of mixed traffic).
- Workload mix profiles:
  - S1 (latency-sensitive): 60% of requests, median tokens 8, 90th tokens 12
  - S2 (throughput-heavy): 35% of requests, median tokens 120, 90th tokens 512
  - S3 (edge large): 5% of requests, streaming long generations (2000+ tokens)
- Baselines: current adaptive timeouts (v1), hybrid-size-timeout policy (v2). New experiment: anchored-batchlets with probe (v3).

Key parameters explored:
- anchor_flush_ms: 15, 30, 50, 80
- anchor_token_reservation_pct: 5%, 10%, 20%
- probe_trigger_p99_ms: 250, 300, 400
- probe_ramp_duration_seconds: 10, 30, 60
- preempt_token_pct_per_slot: 10%, 20%
- slot_length_ms: 10, 20 (unchanged for most runs)

Metrics collected (aggregated per 5m window):
- p50/p90/p95/p99/p999 latency (ms) for end-to-end request completion
- tokens/sec GPU-level and avg GPU utilization
- KV cache hit ratio (since cache hits change batch composition)
- percent slots with preemption
- mean batch size (tokens and requests)

Representative run notes (selected):
Run A (anchor_flush_ms=30, reservation=10%, probe_trigger=300, ramp=30s, preempt=10%):
- p50: unchanged vs baseline (~35ms)
- p95: -12ms
- p99: -48ms (from 540ms -> 492ms)
- p999: -160ms (740ms -> 580ms)
- throughput tokens/sec: -1.8%
- GPU util: -2.4pp (from 78.6% -> 76.2%)
- slot preemptions: 3.2%
Notes: Good tail improvements with modest throughput loss. Probe ramp tended to trigger only during 8/10 observed burst windows; decay time 30s allowed tail to stabilize without oscillation.

Run B (anchor_flush_ms=80, reservation=20%, probe_trigger=250, preempt=20%):
- p99: -120ms
- p999: -300ms
- throughput tokens/sec: -8.9%
- GPU util: -11.1pp
Notes: Extreme anchor reservation reduces tail but at heavy cost to utilization. Observed starvation of S2 workload during continuous bursts. Not acceptable for mixed-tenant prod.

Run C (anchor_flush_ms=15, reservation=5%, probe_trigger=400, ramp=10s, preempt=10%):
- p99: -20ms
- p999: -40ms
- throughput tokens/sec: -0.5%
Notes: Very lightweight anchors provide small tail wins with negligible throughput impact. Probe trigger needs to be conservative (higher threshold) to avoid frequent micro-reroutes during background noise.

Profiling artifacts and bottleneck observations:
- CPU scheduling overhead: assigning requests to anchors adds ~0.7-1.2us/request of scheduler CPU time; negligible compared to token generation in long requests but measurable at 10k rps small-request load.
- Lock contention: single-slot metadata lock became a hotspot under high preemption rates; sharding the slot metadata by token-range removed a 12% latency amplification at p99.
- GPU kernels: no change in kernel runtime for identical batch sizes, but observed more small-batch kernel invocations in high-anchor runs, increasing kernel launch overhead (visible in nvtx traces).
- KV cache: smaller anchored batches had slightly higher cache hit ratio for short-prefix reuse, offsetting some throughput loss in S1.

Operational signals to care about (what to surface in Console):
- anchor pressure metric: fraction of requests that are currently anchored and waiting > anchor_flush_ms/2.
- probe firing rate: how often probe increases fairness in last 5m (count).
- preemption rate per slot.
- delta GPU utilization vs baseline over rolling 1h.

Conclusions so far:
- Middle-ground settings (anchor_flush_ms 30-50ms, reservation 8-12%, probe_trigger 300ms, ramp 30s) give best p99/p999 improvements with <3% throughput loss in our mixed traces.
- Very aggressive anchoring helps tail but unacceptably impacts throughput and causes downstream resource contention.
- Anchors combine well with our KV prefix caching — small anchored batches improve cache friendliness.
- Need a scheduler lock redesign (per-shard slot metadata) before enabling high preemption scenarios in prod.

Next actions / TODOs:
- [Ethan] Spike on slot metadata sharding - PR and microbench (JIRA-ENG-2205) by 2024-11-10.
- [Marta] Add anchor pressure and probe firing metrics to Console (instrument + dashboard) - demo by 2024-12-01.
- [Priya] Run a 24h continuous replay with production traffic (weekend low-risk) with middle-ground config and collect promos/alerts. Schedule: 2024-12-07.
- Create a Canary rollout plan for Dedicated customers with ability to opt-out. Draft policy + comms by 2024-12-15.

Open questions / risks:
- How should we auto-tune reservation_pct? Candidate: proportional to short-request fraction in last 5m, but reacts poorly to quick swings.
- Interaction with autoscaling: Anchors reduce short-term throughput; autoscaler could overreact if not smoothed. Need to introduce an anchor-aware scale metric.
- Billing and fairness: Anchoring may favor SLA classes; need policy for multi-tenant fairness and cost alignment.

Appendix: experiment artifacts and links
- Replay ids used: replay-2024-08-12-3h, replay-2024-09-22-1h
- NVTX traces: gs://redwood-experiments/anchored-batchlets/runA_nvtx.zip
- Perf scripts used: experiments/anchored-batchlets/run-suite.sh (git PR#4523)

Notes to self:
- When writing up for blog/benchmark, avoid marketing claims about absolute single-digit ms wins; focus on tradeoffs and observability knobs.
- Keep the default conservative in prod; provide a "latency aggressive" config for latency-first tenants behind a feature flag.

End of playbook.
